note: The cliff between the sixth circle and the seventh, where the violent are punished. The only way down is a slope of fallen rock.

quote: that landslide which struck the Adige's flank
note: A huge ancient rockslide in the valley of the river Adige, south of Trent in northern Italy, usually identified as the Slavini di Marco near Rovereto. Dante may have seen it in his years of exile, when he stayed at Verona, further down the same river.

context: He guards the circle of the violent. Half man and half beast, he is an image of what violence makes of a human being.

note: Pasiphae, queen of Crete, desired a bull. The craftsman Daedalus built her a hollow wooden cow to hide in, and so she conceived the Minotaur. The lustful recall her as a warning in Purgatorio 26.
Rage with no outlet turns on itself, as with Filippo Argenti in Canto 8.

context: Medieval writers gave the ancient king a title of their own time. Virgil taunts the Minotaur with the name of the man who killed him.

note: Ariadne, daughter of Pasiphae and King Minos, and so the Minotaur's half-sister. She fell in love with Theseus and gave him the thread that led him back out of the labyrinth.
Dante's living body. The shades who pass this way weigh nothing and never shift a stone.
When the witch Erichtho sent him to the bottom of Hell, soon after his death in 19 BC (Canto 9). The cliff was still whole then.

quote: He came who carried off the mighty spoil
note: Christ, who came down after the Crucifixion and took the righteous dead out of Limbo (see Inferno 4). The Gospel says the earth quaked and rocks split when he died (Matthew 27:51). Dante has that earthquake reach Hell and break its cliffs.

context: Here the name is Lucifer's own. The souls Christ took were plunder carried off from Hell's king.

quote: the universe was moved by love
note: Virgil, a pagan, felt the earthquake and explained it with Greek philosophy. He is more right than he knows: it was love that shook Hell, the love shown in Christ's death.

context: In his teaching, Strife keeps the four elements apart and so gives the world its shape. When Love wins, everything is drawn back into one formless mass: chaos.

note: The same earthquake left other ruins in Hell. One is the broken bridge over the ditch of the hypocrites, which the devils lie about in Inferno 21.

context: The first ring of the seventh circle. Those who spilled the blood of others stand in boiling blood, each sunk as deep as his guilt.

quote: Oh blind greed! Oh insane wrath
note: The two roots of violence against others. Greed makes robbers and plunderers. Wrath makes murderers. Tyrants are driven by both.
The river is a ring that runs all the way around the seventh circle. Dante sees one arc of it.

context: Like the Minotaur, they join a human to a beast. They patrol the bank like a troop of mounted archers and keep the violent in their place.
The captain of the troop. Virgil will speak only to him.
Dejanira was the wife of Hercules. The revenge Nessus took was the poisoned blood he gave her as he died, which years later killed Hercules.

note: Head bowed in thought. Dante sets the wise Chiron apart from the others by his stillness.

A centaur named by the Latin poets in the story of the wedding feast of the Lapiths, where the drunken centaurs tried to carry off the women and a battle broke out. Dante recalls that fight in Purgatorio 24.
Each sinner is sunk to a depth that matches his guilt, from the eyebrows to the ankles. Rise higher, and the centaurs shoot.
Chiron has noticed the stones shifting under Dante's feet. He is the first to see that this visitor has a body.
Where the man's torso meets the horse's body. Virgil, standing, reaches only that high.

context: She left the songs of Heaven to come down to Limbo and send Virgil to Dante's rescue (Inferno 2).

note: Neither of them belongs in this circle of robbers and men of violence. They are passing through under orders.
Shades can cross the boiling stream without touching it. Dante needs to be carried.
The worst of the violent, sunk deepest. They took both lives and goods, and from whole peoples.

Most likely Alexander the Great (356–323 BC), whom some of the Latin historians Dante read painted as a bloodthirsty conqueror. Because Dante praises him elsewhere, some readers prefer Alexander of Pherae, a cruel Greek tyrant whom Cicero pairs with Dionysius.
Dionysius the Elder, tyrant of Syracuse in Sicily from 405 to 367 BC, a byword for cruelty and suspicion in ancient writers. His son of the same name ruled after him.

Obizzo II d'Este, marquis of Ferrara, a Guelph lord who died in 1293. Rumor said his son and heir Azzo had smothered him. Dante has Nessus confirm it ("truly"), and calls the son a stepson, perhaps to mark the crime as unnatural, perhaps to hint he was a bastard.
Dante has looked to Virgil to confirm what the centaur says. Virgil tells him to trust Nessus, who knows this river.
The murderers, one step less guilty than the tyrants.

In church, during Mass. In 1271, at Viterbo, Guy de Montfort stabbed Prince Henry of Cornwall, a cousin of the future Edward I of England, to avenge his father Simon de Montfort, killed fighting the English crown in 1265. He stands apart because the murder was also a sacrilege.

quote: the heart still honored on the Thames
note: Henry's heart was reported to have been taken to London and kept in a golden vessel, at Westminster Abbey or on London Bridge.
Dante names none of them. Readers have assumed they are men of violence from the Italy of his own day.
The ford, where the blood is ankle-deep. Dante crosses on the centaur's back, though he doesn't say so.

quote: on the other side it grows deeper
note: Since the river is a ring, it deepens again beyond the ford, round to the place of the tyrants where the poets first saw it.
King of the Huns, who ravaged Europe and invaded Italy in 452. He died the next year. He was known as the Scourge of God, and Dante believed, wrongly, that he had destroyed Florence (Inferno 13).

Either Pyrrhus, king of Epirus (319–272 BC), who invaded Italy and fought the Romans, or Achilles' son Pyrrhus, who butchered old King Priam at the altar when Troy fell, in the Aeneid. Commentators are divided.
Probably Sextus Pompey, son of Pompey the Great, who turned to piracy after his father's defeat and is condemned for it by Lucan. Some prefer Sextus Tarquin, who raped Lucretia (see Inferno 4).

quote: Rinier da Corneto and Rinier Pazzo
note: Two highway robbers of Dante's century. Rinier da Corneto preyed on the roads north of Rome. Rinier Pazzo, a nobleman of the upper Arno valley, was excommunicated for attacking and robbing a party of churchmen.
